growth_story.headline: A war-wrecked economy rebuilt fast, then settled into slower, steadier growth as emigration shrank the population and reforms stalled.
growth_story.arc: The 1992–1995 war wrecked the economy, and donor-funded rebuilding after the Dayton peace drove a rebound: income per person grew 15.3 percent a year over 1991–1998, with a peak of 47.8 percent in 1996. From 1999 to 2008 growth slowed to 5.7 percent a year as rebuilding gave way to an expansion that the IMF later said came with growing external and internal imbalances. The global crisis ended that era: income per person fell 1.3 percent in 2009, and growth has averaged 3.4 percent a year since, with another dip of 1.7 percent in 2020 and a 9.2 percent rebound in 2021. In recent years growth has leaned on household spending, lifted by wage and benefit rises, while heavy emigration has shrunk the population. Income per person reached a new high in 2025, and growth over 2016–2025 averaged 4.1 percent a year, up from 3.8 percent over 2006–2015.

threads.title: War and donor-led rebuilding
threads.text: During the 1992–1995 war, output fell to a small fraction of its pre-war level. A large rebuilding program followed, and by 2000 most housing, roads and power supplies had been restored. Even so, the World Bank found that output in 1999 was still well short of where it had been before the war.

citations.quote: By 1994 the gross domestic product (GDP) and GDP per capita had plummeted to less than 20 percent of the pre-war level

citations.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina: Post-Conflict Reconstruction and the Transition to a Market Economy (An OED Evaluation of World Bank Support)

threads.title: Boom with imbalances, then crisis
threads.text: Growth in the 2000s was strong but came with growing imbalances, and credit to the private sector climbed from 47.8 to 65.6 percent of GDP between 2006 and 2008. When the global crisis hit, demand for exports dropped and foreign investment dried up, pulling down private investment. Income per person fell 1.3 percent in 2009 and growth stayed slower afterwards.

citations.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina: Staff Report for the First Review Under the Stand-By Arrangement (IMF Country Report No. 10/101)
citations.quote: Following several years of strong growth increasingly accompanied by external and internal imbalances, economic activity in Bosnia and Herzegovina (BiH) began to decelerate

citations.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina: Staff Report for the First Review Under the Stand-By Arrangement (IMF Country Report No. 10/101)
citations.quote: The precipitous drop in demand for BiH’s exports and the drying up of foreign direct investment triggered a sharp decline in private investment.

threads.title: Emigration and a shrinking workforce
threads.text: Emigration has cut the population sharply: the World Bank finds that net outflows have shrunk it a great deal since 2001, and because those who leave are mostly of working age, the labor supply has shrunk even faster. The IMF says the departure of young workers has left a high share of dependents, a long-term risk to public finances.

citations.title: International Mobility as a Development Strategy: Bosnia and Herzegovina Country Report
citations.quote: Since the migrant population tends to be of working age, these outflows have led to an even faster reduction in the labor supply.

threads.title: Consumption and public spending
threads.text: Household spending has carried recent growth, lifted by minimum wage rises, while investment and exports have been weak. Since 2022, large increases in social benefits and public wages have raised public debt. The IMF reports falling industrial output and export capacity alongside sharply rising labor costs.

threads.title: Stable anchors, stalled reforms
threads.text: A currency board tied to the euro, efficient collection of indirect taxes and the prospect of joining the EU have kept the economy stable since the war. The IMF says political division has slowed reforms, including those tied to EU accession. The World Bank says growth since 2015 has been too slow to close the income gap with the EU.

since_last_year.text: Growth slowed in 2025. In its July 2026 report, the IMF says higher energy costs and weaker demand abroad, both linked to the Middle East conflict, outweighed strong consumption and public spending, and it expects inflation to rise in 2026. In the data, income per person grew 2.9 percent in 2025, down from 3.9 percent in 2024.

citations.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release and Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/205)
citations.quote: after slowing to 2.1 percent in 2025, as the Middle East conflict—through higher energy costs and weaker external demand—offset strong consumption and fiscal support

citations.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release and Staff Report (IMF Country Report No. 26/205)
citations.quote: Driven by higher fuel prices and expansionary fiscal policy, inflation is projected to rise to 5.4 percent in 2026 from 4 percent in 2025.

growth_story.tension: There are two gaps. First, the World Bank says output by 1994 had fallen far below its pre-war level, but the data series shows income per person in 1994 above its 1990 level, after falls of 9.5 percent in 1991 and 1.5 percent in 1992. The series may miss much of the wartime collapse, and the 15.3 percent average for 1991–1998 mostly reflects fast growth from 1994 to 1998, from a very low starting point. Second, the data show income per person growing 4.1 percent a year over 2016–2025 and reaching a new high in 2025, while the World Bank calls growth since 2015 too slow to close the gap with the EU, and the IMF calls growth weak. Their figures are for the whole economy, and part of the gap is the shrinking population: when people leave, income per person can rise even if the economy as a whole grows slowly.
